1121.event: Around 1882 the French sculptor Auguste Rodin designed a pair of embracing lovers for his great bronze doorway The Gates of Hell, based on Paolo and Francesca from Dante's Divine Comedy. In 1886 he removed the group from the door because its mood of happiness did not suit the project, exhibited it on its own in 1887, and the public named it The Kiss. The French state commissioned a large marble version in 1888, which Rodin carved over nearly ten years and exhibited in 1898; it is now in the Musée Rodin in Paris.
1121.explanation: The Kiss became one of the most famous sculptures in the world and a lasting symbol of tender love.
1121.tie_back: The kural says the sweetness of the beloved's kiss is like milk mixed with honey, and Rodin's The Kiss is the best-known work of art devoted to that very moment of sweetness.
1121._accuracy_note: The kiss is the kural's subject, but a sculpture cannot show its sweetness, and the kural's milk-and-honey image is not echoed in the work.

1122.event_title: The pair statue of King Menkaure and his queen
1122.place: Giza, Egypt; now in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, United States
1122.event: During Egypt's Fourth Dynasty, sculptors carved a nearly life-size statue in greywacke showing King Menkaure standing beside a queen, probably his principal wife. The queen stands with one arm around his waist and her other hand on his arm, and the two figures share one base and back pillar. Excavators led by George Reisner found the statue in Menkaure's valley temple at Giza in January 1910, and it is now in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
1122.explanation: The statue is a masterpiece of Old Kingdom art and one of the earliest images of a couple shown as an affectionate pair.
1122.tie_back: The kural says the bond between the lovers is like the bond between body and life, and this statue, carved more than 4,000 years ago, presents king and queen as one joined form, standing together for eternity.
1122._accuracy_note: The image of two beings joined as one fits the kural's body-and-life bond, but it is a royal statue whose exact purpose and queen's identity are not fully known.

1123.event_title: The Prince of Wales sends Maria Fitzherbert a portrait of his eye
1123.event: George, Prince of Wales (later King George IV), fell in love with Maria Fitzherbert, a twice-widowed Catholic, in 1784, but the law and his father barred him from marrying her, and she left for the Continent. In November 1785 he sent her a proposal accompanied not by a ring but by a miniature painting of his own eye, made by the miniaturist Richard Cosway. She returned, and in December 1785 they married in a secret ceremony that was not legally valid because it lacked royal consent.
1123.explanation: The gift helped start a fashion for lover's eye miniatures, small portraits of a single eye worn as private love tokens.
1123.tie_back: The kural's lover tells the little image in his pupil to leave so that only his beloved may dwell in his eye; the prince built his love token on the same idea of the eye as love's dwelling place, sending his own eye so that his gaze would always be with her.
1123._accuracy_note: The eye as the home of love links them, but the prince sent his own eye to her rather than clearing his eye to hold only her image.

1124.event_title: The wife of Yi Eung-tae writes a farewell letter
1124.event: In 1586 Yi Eung-tae, a member of the Goseong Yi clan in Andong, Korea, died young, and his pregnant wife wrote him a letter in the Korean script, addressing him as the father of their son Won. In it she wrote that she could not live without him and wanted to go to him, asked how their unborn child should know its father, and begged him to come and speak to her in her dreams. The letter was laid in his grave, where archaeologists found it centuries later, and it helped them identify him.
1124.explanation: The letter is one of the most moving personal documents to survive from Joseon Korea, and it shows a deep marriage of love at a time when such feelings were rarely written down.
1124.tie_back: The kural says the beloved is like life to the soul when near and like death when parted, and this young widow's letter says almost exactly that: without her husband she felt she could not go on living.
1124._accuracy_note: Very close in feeling and almost in wording, though the parting here is death rather than a lover's leaving, and the speaker is the wife, not the husband.

1125.event_title: Su Shi dreams of his late wife Wang Fu
1125.event: In 1075 the Song dynasty poet and official Su Shi wrote a lyric to the tune Jiang Chengzi after dreaming of his first wife, Wang Fu, who had died ten years earlier at about twenty-seven. The poem says that for ten years the living and the dead have known nothing of each other, and that although he does not try to think of her, he cannot forget her. In the dream he returns home and sees her, and he wakes in grief.
1125.explanation: The poem is one of the most famous elegies in Chinese literature, admired for expressing lasting love in very plain words.
1125.tie_back: The kural's lover says he would remember his beloved's qualities if he ever forgot them, but he never forgets; Su Shi's poem turns on the same paradox, saying he does not set out to remember his wife because he has never been able to forget her.
1125._accuracy_note: The remembering-without-forgetting paradox is almost identical; the difference is that Su Shi's beloved had died.

1126.event_title: Calpurnia keeps Pliny's writings in his place
1126.event: The Roman senator and author Pliny the Younger wrote letters to his young wife Calpurnia while they were apart, and some were included in his published collection of letters. In one of them (Letters 6.7) he replies to her complaint that she misses him terribly and comforts herself by embracing his writings instead of him and putting them in the place where he usually sits. He answers that he rereads her letters again and again, and asks her to write as often as she can.
1126.explanation: Pliny's letters to Calpurnia are among the rare surviving glimpses of affection inside a Roman marriage.
1126.tie_back: The kural's heroine says her lover never leaves her eyes, so fine that even blinking cannot harm him; Calpurnia, too, kept her absent husband constantly before her by placing his words where he used to be.
1126._accuracy_note: A wife keeping her absent husband always present fits, but she does it through his writings rather than an inner image held in her eyes.

1127.event_title: Juliette Drouet gives up the stage for Victor Hugo
1127.event: The French actress Juliette Drouet began her relationship with the writer Victor Hugo in 1833, and in the mid-1830s she gave up her stage career to devote herself to him. For about fifty years, until her death in 1883, she remained his companion, travelled with him and copied out his works for his publishers. She wrote him at least one letter a day, about 22,000 in all.
1127.explanation: Her letters to Hugo form one of the largest bodies of correspondence in the history of literature.
1127.tie_back: The kural's heroine gives up even the daily adornment of kohl on her eyes so that nothing hides the lover who lives there; Drouet gave up the public life of the stage and ordered her whole life around Hugo.
1127._accuracy_note: Next-best only: giving up something of one's own for the beloved fits in spirit, but the kural's specific, playful reason, not wanting to hide him in her eyes, has no parallel here.

1128.event_title: Lady Dervorguilla keeps her husband's heart and founds Sweetheart Abbey
1128.place: New Abbey, Dumfries and Galloway, Scotland
1128.event: When John Balliol died in 1268, his widow, Lady Dervorguilla of Galloway, had his heart embalmed and placed in a casket of ivory (one account says silver and ivory), which she kept with her. In 1273 she founded a Cistercian abbey in his memory, which the monks named Dulce Cor, Latin for sweet heart. When she died in 1289 she was buried before the abbey's high altar with her husband's heart.
1128.explanation: The ruined abbey, still known as Sweetheart Abbey, remains one of Scotland's best-known monuments to married love.
1128.tie_back: The kural's heroine keeps her lover so truly within her heart that she fears hot food might burn him, and Dervorguilla kept her husband's heart close to her for more than twenty years and was buried holding it.
1128._accuracy_note: Keeping the beloved, quite literally, at one's heart fits, but the kural is a living lover's tender joke, while this is a widow's memorial.

1129.event_title: Chopin and George Sand's winter in Majorca
1129.event: In November 1838 the composer Frédéric Chopin and the novelist George Sand travelled to Majorca, and from mid-December they lived in rented cells in the former Carthusian monastery at Valldemossa. Chopin fell seriously ill with a cough, and local people, fearing his illness was contagious, turned against the couple: one landlord made them leave, and villagers refused to sell them supplies. Sand cared for him while he completed his 24 Preludes, and they left in February 1839; she later described the stay in A Winter in Majorca (1842).
1129.explanation: The winter produced some of Chopin's greatest music, even while the local community judged the couple harshly from the outside.
1129.tie_back: The kural's heroine protests that the town wrongly judges her lover from what it sees on the surface; the Majorcans likewise judged Chopin and Sand only by appearances, while the couple's devotion went on unseen inside the monastery.
1129._accuracy_note: Next-best only: outsiders misjudging a couple is the link, but the town here feared illness rather than calling the lover unloving, and the kural's sleepless heroine has no parallel.

1130.event_title: George IV is buried wearing Maria Fitzherbert's portrait
1130.event: George IV and Maria Fitzherbert, whom he had secretly and invalidly married in 1785, finally parted in 1811, after which she lived privately on an allowance. Yet when George IV died in 1830 he was wearing a locket with her miniature portrait around his neck, and at his own request he was buried with it at his breast.
1130.explanation: The burial revealed that a bond the public had long thought finished had stayed with the king to the end.
1130.tie_back: The kural's heroine says the town calls her lover distant and unloving though he dwells joyfully in her heart; the world believed George IV had long left Maria behind, but her portrait stayed over his heart until his death.
1130._accuracy_note: Strong on the gap between outward separation and inner devotion, though the roles are reversed (he kept her in his heart) and the separation was largely his own doing.
